Two hypotheses

The church of San Leonardo, June. Reflectography has revealed, under the eighteenth-century Madonna, a different drawing: another face, another position of the hands. Chiara and Karl discuss it in front of the screen, while Pietro listens.
The drawing underneath is completely different. Let's suppose it's a fourteenth-century Madonna.
There are two hypotheses. First hypothesis: the eighteenth-century painter painted over an old, damaged Madonna.
And the second?
He reused an old panel, without knowing what was underneath. If that were so, the wood would be fourteenth-century but the drawing would be unfinished.
And how do you work out which of the two is true?
You verify. First, the age of the wood, with dendrochronology. You count the rings, as on a felled tree.
Then the paint. Should there be paint underneath too, and not just the drawing, the first hypothesis would be confirmed.
And what if the data disproved both?
Then we'd make a third. That's how science works: a hypothesis holds until nobody manages to disprove it.
And if the first were true? Would we remove the eighteenth century to see the fourteenth?
That's not a scientific question, Karl. It's a dilemma. And no instrument gives the answer.

They all require the subjunctive, because they talk about something unproven. After verification you switch to the indicative: "È dimostrato che il legno È del Trecento."
2. The formal condition: qualora, nel caso in cui

"Qualora" does NOT mean "whenever" and never takes the indicative: "qualora fosse", "qualora sia", not "qualora è".

La Madonna dai due volti

The open worksite in the church of San Leonardo began on the first Saturday in June, at nine in the morning, with a small ceremony that don Paolo had insisted on at all costs. In front of the altar, where until the day before there had been only empty pews, there was now a metal scaffold four metres high, covered with a white sheet, and around it an enclosure of red ropes with a sign handwritten by Davide: "Restoration in progress. Please look. Please don't touch." In front of the enclosure, that first morning, there were seventeen people: don Paolo, the village mayor, two nuns, about ten elderly parishioners and three children who had come only because someone had promised them sweets. Don Paolo counted them twice. "Seventeen," he said to Karl, his eyes moist. "At Easter there were twelve."

The work of the first days was mainly analysis. Before touching the Madonna, you had to get to know her. Chiara and Karl photographed her in every possible light: normal light, raking light, ultraviolet, infrared. Pietro, who had finished school in June and could be at the worksite every Saturday, acted as guide for the visitors, explaining in simple words what was happening. Davide, sitting on a stool at the back of the nave, drew everything for the little book the diocese would print at the end of the work. On the third Saturday, while Karl was setting up the camera for infrared reflectography, Pietro was explaining to a group of German tourists what an underdrawing was. "It's the sketch the painter makes on the panel before painting," he said in English. "Like the rough draft of an essay." At that very moment Karl called him. His voice sounded strange.

On the computer screen, connected to the camera, the Madonna could be seen as nobody had ever seen her. The infrared passed through the layers of eighteenth-century paint and showed, underneath, the black lines of the underdrawing. But the drawing didn't match the painting. The eighteenth-century Madonna looked at the child, her head tilted to the right and her hands joined in prayer. The drawing underneath showed another face, longer, sterner, with the head tilted to the left, looking straight at whoever was looking at the picture. And the hands weren't joined: one held the child, the other pointed at something below, outside the panel. Chiara came running, looked at the screen and sat down on the altar step without saying anything. The German tourists applauded, without really knowing why.

That evening, in don Paolo's parish house, around a wooden table covered with printed photographs, the discussion began. Chiara and Karl formulated two hypotheses. The first: an eighteenth-century painter had found in the church a fourteenth-century Madonna badly damaged, perhaps by damp or by a fire, and instead of restoring it had repainted it completely, according to the taste of his time. The second: the painter had simply reused an old panel, bought or found somewhere, on which someone in the fourteenth century had begun a drawing without ever finishing it. "Should the first be true," Chiara explained, "under the eighteenth century there would still be a medieval painting, perhaps partly preserved. Should the second be true, there would only be a drawing. And an old panel."

Don Paolo listened with his hands clasped on the table, without interrupting. Then he asked something nobody expected. "And what if both were true?" Chiara looked at him in surprise. The old priest smiled. "I'm not a scientist," he said. "But I've read many books on the history of the diocese. And in the eighteenth century, here, there was no money. A country painter would never have thrown away a panel. And he would never have covered a beautiful work, if it had still been beautiful." Karl wrote the sentence in his notebook. "It's a third hypothesis," he said. "The old Madonna was damaged, and the painter knew it. He covered it out of respect, not out of ignorance." Chiara nodded slowly. "Let's suppose don Paolo is right," she said. "How do we verify it?"

The verification required three experiments, and three weeks. The first was dendrochronology. An expert from the University of Florence, Dr Lapini, came to the church with a special microscope and photographed the edge of the panel, where the wood was exposed. "Trees grow one ring a year," he explained to the visitors, who that Saturday numbered thirty-two. "Warm, rainy years, wide rings. Cold, dry years, narrow rings. Every century has its own sequence, like a barcode. If we compare the rings of this panel with the sequences we know, we can tell when the tree was felled." Pietro translated the explanation for a Dutch couple. Then he added, on his own: "It's like reading a tree's diary." Dr Lapini turned and looked at him. "I'm stealing that sentence," he said.

That evening Chiara phoned Professor Ruggeri, in Rome, to tell him everything. Ruggeri listened in silence, then gave her a single piece of advice, the same he had given Pietro on the quay at Marsaxlokk. "Don't fall in love with any hypothesis," he said. "Not even the priest's, which is the most beautiful. A beautiful hypothesis is the most dangerous, because you want it to be true." Then he explained how he would set up the verification: for each hypothesis, first write down what you should find should it be true, and only afterwards go and look. "If you search before deciding what you're searching for," he said, "you always find what you want to find." Chiara wrote the sentence on a sheet of paper and taped it to the worksite computer. The next day, Karl added underneath, in pen: "Signed: a professor who was once sceptical."

The preliminary results arrived after ten days. The tree had been felled between 1318 and 1330. The wood was poplar, as in almost all Tuscan panels of that period. The panel was therefore fourteenth-century: that was now proven. But dendrochronology alone wasn't enough to distinguish between the hypotheses. A fourteenth-century panel could have on it a fourteenth-century drawing, finished or unfinished. The second experiment was needed: to find out whether under the eighteenth century there was paint too, and not just drawing. So Karl suggested using the fluorescence spectrometer, the same one Ruggeri had used in Malta. "Should we find gold, lapis lazuli, cinnabar under the eighteenth-century paint," he said, "we'll know there's a real painting underneath. A drawing on its own has no colours."

The spectrometer found everything. Under the azure sky of the eighteenth century, made with cheap Prussian blue, there was a layer of lapis lazuli, the most precious blue of the Middle Ages, the one that cost more than gold. Under the halo painted yellow there was real gold, in leaf. And under the red cloak there was cinnabar. But there was also something nobody expected. In some places, especially at the bottom, the spectrometer found no medieval paint: it found only the gesso of the ground, and traces of charcoal. "The old painting isn't there any more," said Chiara, looking at the graphs. "It has fallen off. Perhaps burnt, perhaps ruined by water. The eighteenth-century painter found a very beautiful Madonna, but with enormous holes." Don Paolo, watching from behind the red ropes, made the sign of the cross. "Then I was right," he said quietly. "And you were right too."

The third experiment was done by no instrument. It was done by a ninety-two-year-old lady called Nunzia. She came to the worksite every Saturday, leaning on a stick, and always sat on the same pew, in the front row, without talking to anyone. On the fifth Saturday, while Pietro was explaining to the visitors the story of the hidden drawing, Signora Nunzia raised her hand. Everyone turned round. "The Madonna with two faces," she said in a thin voice. "My grandmother used to tell me about it when I was a little girl. She said the Madonna of San Leonardo had two faces. One for feast days and one for days of sorrow. She said the face of sorrow had burned in a fire, many years before, and that a painter had covered it with a new face, so that people wouldn't cry looking at it."

Silence fell in the church. Chiara went up to Signora Nunzia and knelt beside the pew. She asked her whether her grandmother had ever told her when the fire had been. The lady thought for a long time, with her eyes closed. "In the time of the French," she said at last. "My grandmother always said that. In the time of the French the sacristy burned, and the fire reached the altar." Don Paolo got up abruptly and went to the parish house. He came back half an hour later, with an old leather-bound parish register, covered in dust. He opened it at a page marked with a ribbon. It said, in old and ornate Italian: "On the 3rd day of April 1709, fire broke out in the sacristy, and burned a great part of the high altar, and the sacred image of Our Lady was much harmed."

"1709," said Karl. "It wasn't the French. But for a grandmother born in the nineteenth century, everything that had happened before Napoleon was 'in the time of the French'." Chiara laughed, but her eyes were moist. The three hypotheses, the legend and the register now said the same thing. In the fourteenth century a Sienese painter had painted a stern Madonna, with her hand pointing down. In 1709 a fire had badly damaged it. A few years later a country painter, with little money and much respect, had covered it with a new Madonna, gentler, more suited to the taste of his time, leaving underneath what remained of the old one. "Everything suggests that's how it went," said Chiara, carefully using Ruggeri's words. "It remains to be verified who the fourteenth-century painter was. But that, perhaps, we'll never know."

At that point the dilemma arose. Karl raised it one evening, in the parish house, when everyone was already tired. "Should we decide to remove the eighteenth century," he said, "we could see what remains of the fourteenth. A stern face, a hand, a piece of cloak, the gold of the halo. Perhaps a masterpiece." Chiara looked at him. "And we would lose the eighteenth-century Madonna for ever," she replied. "The one the people here have prayed to for three hundred years. The one Signora Nunzia's grandmother saw every Sunday." Matei and Giulia, who had come from Florence that afternoon to see the results, said nothing. It was the kind of decision no instrument could take. A restoration can be done in many ways. But some choices are not reversible. "Let's ask the people who pray to her," Giulia said at last. "She's theirs."

So, the following Saturday, don Paolo did something that had never been seen in a country church: a parish assembly with the infrared photographs projected on the white wall of the nave. Sixty-eight people came. Some hadn't set foot in church for years. Chiara explained the two possibilities in simple words, without technical jargon: remove the new Madonna to see the remains of the old one, or leave the new Madonna and show the old one in another way. There was a long discussion, sometimes heated. A young farmer said a fourteenth-century masterpiece would bring tourists and money to the village. A retired schoolteacher said the Madonna was not a tourist attraction. Then Signora Nunzia raised her hand again, and again everyone fell silent.

"The eighteenth-century painter," she said, "covered the face of sorrow so that people wouldn't cry. He was kind. Now you want to uncover it. But the sorrow has passed, and the new face has kept us company for three hundred years. I prayed in front of that face when my husband died, and when my son died. Don't take it away from me." She stopped, caught her breath. "But I would like to see the old one. Just once, before I die. If there's a way to see it without taking the other one away from us, do it." Nobody in the church spoke. Then Karl stood up. "There is a way," he said. "It's called digital reconstruction. With the infrared photographs and the spectrometer data we can reconstruct the fourteenth-century Madonna on the computer, with her colours. And we can print her, life-size."

The decision was taken by a show of hands. Sixty-six votes to leave the eighteenth-century Madonna and make the digital reconstruction. Two votes against, including the young farmer's, who at the end of the assembly nevertheless went up to Karl to ask whether he could help put up the print. The restoration continued as planned: cleaning the varnish, consolidating the wood, small reversible retouches in the areas where the eighteenth-century paint had lifted. Every Saturday the visitors increased. In July there were ninety. In August, a hundred and forty. Schools from the nearby villages came, a group of pilgrims from Assisi, a regional television crew. And one Saturday in July, as he had promised, albeit two months late, Dr Ferraris came from Milan, paid the symbolic one-euro ticket and flatly refused to go in for free.

Ferraris stayed at the church all morning. He listened to Pietro explaining the analyses, looked at the infrared photographs, asked Karl technical questions about the spectrometer that showed he had done his homework. Then he sat in the front row, next to Signora Nunzia, and the two of them talked in low voices for almost an hour, he in his blue coat too warm for July, she with her stick. Nobody found out what they talked about. Before leaving, Ferraris asked for the visitors' book and wrote a long line, in elegant handwriting. When he had gone, Karl went to read it. It said: "I came to see a restoration. I saw a village coming back to church. We work for those who need it: your Ernesto was right, and so was my grandfather." Underneath, in small letters, he had added: "P.S. Signora Nunzia asked me if I'm married. I told her I'm not."

The digital reconstruction was ready in September. Karl had worked on it all summer, in the evenings, in the room with the window onto the courtyard, with Chiara's help for the colours and Davide's for the missing parts, which he had drawn in pencil on the basis of the underdrawing, marking them with light hatching, so that it would be clear they were hypotheses and not certainties. The print, life-size, on light canvas, was hung next to the eighteenth-century Madonna, in the side chapel. On one side the gentle Madonna, looking at the child. On the other the stern Madonna, looking at whoever came into the church and pointing with her hand at something below. Underneath, a panel explained everything: the analyses, the hypotheses, the 1709 register, the legend of Nunzia's grandmother. And at the end, a sentence in italics: "In the current state of knowledge, the fourteenth-century author remains unknown."

Signora Nunzia saw it on the first Saturday in September. She arrived leaning on her stick and on Pietro's arm, who had gone to fetch her from home. She stopped in front of the two Madonnas, side by side, and stayed looking at them for a very long time. Nobody dared disturb her. Then she went up to the reconstruction and looked at the old Madonna's hand, the one pointing down, outside the picture. "What is it pointing at?" she asked Pietro. Pietro didn't know. Nobody knew. It was one of the questions without an answer. But Pietro looked down, in the direction of the hand, and saw that it pointed exactly at the spot in the floor where, according to don Paolo, in the fourteenth century there had been the tomb of the church's founders. He told nobody. He wrote it that evening in the black notebook, with a question mark as big as a page.

When Signora Nunzia turned round, she had tears in her eyes, but she was smiling. "She's beautiful," she said. "Stern, but beautiful. My grandmother was right." Then she turned to the eighteenth-century Madonna and made a small curtsy, as you do to an old friend. "And you're beautiful too," she said to her. "Thank you for staying." Don Paolo, watching the scene from the sacristy door, dried his eyes with his handkerchief. That Saturday, in the church of San Leonardo, there were two hundred and ten people. It was the first time, don Paolo said, that the church had been full since he had arrived, in 1971. At Mass the following Sunday there were fifty-five. It wasn't two hundred. But it was more than the candles.

The bishop arrived at the end of September, for the ceremony closing the worksite. He was accompanied by Monsignor Cappelli, who carried his gigantic calculator under his arm, "just in case". The bishop looked at the two Madonnas for a long time, listened to Chiara explaining the analyses and Karl explaining the reconstruction, then asked to meet Signora Nunzia. They talked for ten minutes, apart from the others, and nobody ever found out what they said. Then the bishop came back in front of everyone and announced that the church of San Leonardo would not be closed. Indeed: from the following year it would have a young curate, to help don Paolo. Monsignor Cappelli, beside him, typed something on his calculator, looked at the result and smiled for the second time in his life, according to Chiara, who was keeping count.

That evening, in the black notebook, Pietro wrote a summary of the summer, as Ruggeri had taught him: first the facts, then the hypotheses, then the questions. "Facts: the wood is from 1318–1330. Under the eighteenth century there are gold, lapis lazuli and cinnabar. In 1709 there was a fire. Hypotheses: a Sienese painter painted the stern Madonna; a country painter covered it out of respect. Everything suggests it's true. Questions: who was the fourteenth-century painter? What is the hand pointing at?" Then he reread the page, and added a line that was neither a fact, nor a hypothesis, nor a question. "Today I understood that science tells you what is under a painting. But it's people who decide what to leave on top."
